rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second or two
why: "for a second" is used here as a vague universal duration marker rather than a real, rendered beat of time.
suggestion: He comes down the hall at a full run and hits her hard enough that she drops the bag, yelling something that isn't words. Then it is words.

rule_name: Subordinate Instead of Chaining With "And" / "Then"
quote: and hits her hard enough that she drops the bag, and he is yelling something
why: three unequal actions (running, hitting, yelling) are strung together with flat "and" coordination instead of a hierarchy.
suggestion: Coming down the hall at a full run, he hits her hard enough that she drops the bag, yelling something that isn't words for a second or two.

rule_name: Dialogue Tag Clutter, Let Action Beats Carry Tone
quote: Ruth says, coming up behind him with her hand already out for the bag
why: the tag is loaded with a participial explanation of circumstance instead of the physical detail getting its own sentence.
suggestion: Ruth comes up behind him, her hand already out for the bag. "You said probably not," she says.

rule_name: Subordinate Instead of Chaining With "And" / "Then"
quote: and Chloe writes it under the name, then leaves four lines and writes Sam's name at the top of the fifth
why: three distinct actions are chained with flat "and"/"then" coordination, giving them equal weight instead of a hierarchy.
suggestion: Ruth gives her the number without asking again. Chloe writes it under the name, then, leaving four lines, writes Sam's name at the top of the fifth.

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction
quote: Nobody in the dining hall asks her where she is from, or what she is good at.
why: reports nobody's reaction as evidence the newcomer's arrival is unremarkable, exactly the construction the rule bans.
suggestion: A boy passes with his tray without slowing down; nobody stops to ask where she's from.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (interiority of non-POV character)
quote: which he seems to think matters a great deal to her
why: the narration attributes an inner belief to Sam, a non-POV character, which STYLE_RULES bans regardless of the hedge.
suggestion: Sam takes her round by the long corridor to show her a window that doesn't shut properly.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (interiority of non-POV character)
quote: Ruth thinks about it
why: the narration reports a non-POV character's (Ruth's) internal cognitive act, which the automatic-fail list requires replacing with a physical action.
suggestion: Ruth tilts her head, "kind of, he's the one who wouldn't do the water thing," and stacks her tray on the rack.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a second
why: "for a second" is used as a generic duration filler rather than a specific rendered moment.
suggestion: Ruth tilts her head, "kind of, he's the one who wouldn't do the water thing,"

rule_name: Keep Narrative Tense Consistent Unless the Break Is Signalled
quote: Chloe knew it was four before Ruth said it, because she counted them herself in the week it happened.
why: the chapter is narrated in present tense; this sentence drops into simple past with no signalled break.
suggestion: Chloe already knows it's four before Ruth says it; she counted them herself the week it happened.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: Chloe knew it was four
why: routes the fact through the perception verb "knew" instead of stating it directly.
suggestion: It was four before Ruth said it — she'd counted them herself in the week it happened.

rule_name: Hedge Where the Character Could Not Know, Cut Filler Everywhere Else
quote: just calls the afternoon
why: "just" softens a plain narrative claim the narrator is entitled to make outright, with nothing being hedged.
suggestion: then two hours in the afternoon that Fen calls the fun ones and everybody else calls the afternoon.

rule_name: Dialogue Tag Clutter, Let Action Beats Carry Tone
quote: Priya says at dinner, reaching past her for the bread
why: the tag is loaded with a location phrase and a participial action instead of splitting the physical detail into its own sentence.
suggestion: Priya reaches past her for the bread at dinner. "He went to the Olympics," she says.

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction
quote: Nobody at the table asks a follow-up question.
why: reports the table's absent reaction to normalise the Olympics fact instead of giving one character an actual response.
suggestion: Priya just reaches for more bread, like she's said it a hundred times before.

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction
quote: Nobody in the room seems surprised by any of this.
why: reports the room's absent reaction as proof the moment is ordinary rather than showing what the other students are doing instead.
suggestion: Two of them are already answering before she's finished the sentence.

rule_name: Repetition as Emphasis, Say It Once
quote: arrives at once, all of it at the same time
why: restates the identical idea ("at once" / "at the same time") twice in the same sentence with no new information added.
suggestion: On Wednesday a whole sentence arrives at once, and she is so pleased with herself that she loses the four that come after it.

rule_name: Use Past Perfect for Action Before the Narrative Present
quote: At camp somebody explained fractions to her and she went away and worked out for herself why you flip the second one
why: narrates an event from before the story's present-tense narrative moment in simple past instead of past perfect, collapsing the two time frames.
suggestion: At camp somebody had explained fractions to her, and she had gone away and worked out for herself why you flip the second one.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (superlatives in narration)
quote: He never does.
why: an absolute superlative claim delivered in narration; the automatic-fail list marks these fine only in dialogue.
suggestion: He hasn't yet.

rule_name: Dialogue Formatting and Typography
quote: any of them, She is behind
why: a comma splice joins two independent clauses, and the word after the comma is stray-capitalized as if starting a new sentence.
suggestion: any of them. She is behind in Spanish, mathematics, writing and history,

rule_name: Invented similes in narration
quote: looks at her like the question is slightly the wrong shape
why: a newly built, writerly comparison delivered by the narrator rather than a character, which the register rule reserves for dialogue or thought.
suggestion: the teacher looks at her for a second before he answers.

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (obvious causal clause)
quote: because in class there is the class
why: a circular, self-evident "because" clause of the kind the automatic-fail list says to cut outright.
suggestion: There is no reading in class, and there is very little in the afternoon, because Ruth is at the next station over with something always going on.

rule_name: Telling After Showing
quote: It is not a question, so Chloe doesn't answer it.
why: explains a fact the punctuation and the exchange already show, narrating the inference instead of trusting the reader to make it.
suggestion: "You got it," Ruth says. "Which way did you go, because there are two ways and one of them is horrible."

rule_name: Trailing clause
quote: which she does not normally manage for anybody
why: a trailing "which" clause tells the reader how to take the preceding image instead of letting Ruth listening without interrupting stand on its own.
suggestion: Ruth listens to the whole thing without interrupting once, then puts her own working up next to it.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the whole thing without interrupting
why: "the whole thing" is listed by name as a phrase that has stopped functioning as language.
suggestion: Ruth listens without interrupting once, then puts her own working up next to it.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: but that's the end of it
why: a near-verbatim match to the reflexive scene-closer the rule explicitly bans ("and that's the end of it").
suggestion: "Their family comes and gets them." (cut the closer)

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: and that's the whole thing
why: "the whole thing" is named directly in the rule's list of phrases that have become wallpaper.
suggestion: "About going, because she came and got him and he didn't want to go."

rule_name: Negative Framing and Minimisation
quote: but it is not that there is less to say
why: defines the phone calls by denying a reading nobody in the scene asserted, instead of stating plainly what is filling the time.
suggestion: but somebody is always waiting behind her, shifting their weight.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: she can hear somebody behind her shifting their weight
why: routes the auditory detail through the perception filter "can hear" instead of rendering the stimulus directly.
suggestion: somebody behind her shifts their weight, the whole time she is talking.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: it takes Chloe a second to work out
why: "a second" is used again as a vague, universal duration marker standing in for the actual beat of realizing something is funny.
suggestion: and Chloe catches up half a beat behind her — it was funny.

rule_name: Thought Reported vs. Thought Rendered
quote: Chloe thinks about it
why: states the fact of cognition without rendering the thought itself, matching the rule's own banned example almost exactly.
suggestion: Happy — the pool, or Ruth, or all of it, she can't get it down to one word before her mother waits her out.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the whole thing including the small islands
why: a third instance of the named crutch phrase "the whole thing" in this chapter alone.
suggestion: Ruth can do the whole map, including the small islands off the top of Scotland,

rule_name: Repetition as Emphasis, Say It Once
quote: "September."
why: a second character repeats the first character's line back verbatim with no new information added by the repeat.
suggestion: "September," Sam says again, like he's checking it off.

rule_name: Subordinate Instead of Chaining With "And" / "Then"
quote: and then she closes it and holds it on her lap for four hundred miles
why: coordinates the closing image with flat "and"/"then" chaining instead of subordinating it, undercutting the weight the last line is meant to carry.
suggestion: In the car Chloe opens the notebook and checks the inside cover, where three names sit with their spellings and numbers written out, before closing it and holding it on her lap for four hundred miles.
